result: ΦStaph1N phage infection of three MRSA strains (MRSA252, MW2, LAC) leads to evolution of phage resistance and dramatic reduction in β-lactam resistance. The phage formed plaques on all three strains but could not eradicate cultures. Phage-resistant survivors showed 10- to 1000-fold reductions in MIC against oxacillin, cefazolin, and amoxicillin+clavulanic acid, but no change against vancomycin or amoxicillin alone. The magnitude of MIC reduction was MOI-dependent and varied by strain.
evaluation: All three reviewers found the experiments convincing. Reviewer 1 stated 'the findings are convincing,' Reviewer 2 noted 'Phage-mediated re-sensitization to antibiotics has been reported previously,' and Reviewer 3 stated 'the experiments carried out are convincing to suggest such in vitro development of sensitivity to the antibiotics.' No concerns were raised about these core phenotypic observations.

result: An evolved phage variant (Evo2) with a single point mutation in ORF141 shows enhanced lytic activity against MW2 and LAC at lower MOIs compared to ΦStaph1N. Evo2 similarly reduces β-lactam resistance in all three MRSA strains and shows broader activity against USA300 clinical isolates, with some strains unable to evolve resistance after 15 challenges.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically noted that 'Authors were also able to "evolve" phage in similar fashion thus showing enhanced virulence against the bacterium,' indicating acceptance of the Evo2 findings. Reviewer 2 acknowledged the work identifies mutations in genes required for phage infection. No concerns were raised about the Evo2 characterization or its effects on antibiotic resistance.

result: Testing of additional phages shows that the phage-antibiotic resistance trade-off is phage-specific. SATA8505 phage produces similar loss of oxacillin resistance in phage-resistant cells, while ΦNM1γ6 (Dubowvirus genus) generates phage resistance without reducing β-lactam resistance.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted a limitation is 'the use of lab strains and a single pair of phages' but stated 'incorporation of clinical isolates would increase the translational relevance of this work it is unlikely to change the conclusions.' The additional phage data (SATA8505 and ΦNM1γ6) addresses this concern by showing the phenomenon is not limited to a single phage, and no reviewer challenged these findings.

result: Whole-genome sequencing reveals that each MRSA strain evolved distinct mutation profiles following phage infection, with no mutations in SCCmec or blaZ loci. MRSA252 evolved mutations in femA; MW2 evolved mutations in transcriptional regulators mgrA and sarA; LAC evolved mutations in arlR and spoVG. Single knockout mutants of these genes were not sufficient to confer phage resistance, suggesting complex mechanisms.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated the work 'improves our knowledge of how mutation in genes required for phage infection confers sensitivity to β-lactams.' Reviewer 2 noted 'Phage-mediated re-sensitization to antibiotics has been reported previously but the underlying mutational analyses have not been described,' highlighting this as a strength. Reviewer 3 stated 'authors carry out DNA sequencing of both evolved bacteria and phage and show mutations occurring in various genes. Overall, the experiments that have been carried out are convincing.'

result: RNA-seq analysis of phage-treated MW2 and LAC shows significant transcriptional changes including upregulation of ebh, urease genes, cell wall maintenance genes (lytN, fmhC), and tarM in MW2, and downregulation of virulence factors (ess locus, staphyloxanthin biosynthesis, quorum sensing genes). No changes in SCCmec or blaZ expression were observed. Some virulence factors like spa (MW2) and lukD/E (LAC) were upregulated.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated the work 'improves our knowledge of how mutation in genes required for phage infection confers sensitivity to β-lactams and alter virulence properties.' Reviewer 3 noted 'the strains also show other changes in their phenotype' beyond antibiotic sensitivity. The RNA-seq data provides mechanistic support for the observed phenotypes, and no reviewer challenged these transcriptional findings.

result: Phage-treated MW2 and LAC show reduced hemolysis on blood agar (4- to 5-fold reduction with ΦStaph1N, more pronounced with Evo2), despite no reduction in hla transcript expression. MRSA252 showed no hemolysis in parental or evolved forms. Evo2 infection of MRSA252 reduced biofilm formation, but no change was observed in MW2 or LAC.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated the work shows how mutations 'alter virulence properties.' Reviewer 3 noted 'the strains also show other changes in their phenotype such as reduced binding to fibrinogen and hemolysis,' and found the experiments 'convincing.' No concerns were raised about the hemolysis or biofilm data.

result: Phage-treated MW2 and LAC displayed reduced clumping/fibrinogen binding compared to parental strains. Evo2 infection resulted in approximately 3-fold reduction in MW2, while both ΦStaph1N and Evo2 produced comparable reductions in LAC.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically mentioned 'reduced binding to fibrinogen' as one of the phenotypic changes and found the experiments convincing. Reviewer 1 noted the work shows how mutations 'alter virulence properties.' No concerns were raised about the clumping data.

result: Checkerboard assays combining phage and oxacillin show strain-specific responses. With Evo2, MRSA252 and MW2 can grow at low phage/antibiotic combinations and evolved cells show both phage resistance and reduced antibiotic resistance. LAC shows no growth with Evo2 regardless of oxacillin. With ΦStaph1N, only MW2 shows growth across combinations, and high oxacillin prevents loss of antibiotic resistance while low oxacillin permits the trade-off.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted 'These studies suggest that phages and antibiotics may target similar pathways in bacteria,' which aligns with the combination therapy findings. Reviewer 3 found the experiments 'convincing.' No concerns were raised about the checkerboard assay data showing the interaction between phage and antibiotic selection pressures.

result: In some cases, Evo2-resistant LAC became sensitized to fosfomycin and daptomycin, and one replicate of Evo2-resistant MRSA252 evolved sensitivity to teicoplanin, suggesting broader effects on antibiotic resistance beyond β-lactams.
evaluation: These findings are presented as exceptions to the general pattern and are supported by data in Table 2. No reviewer challenged these observations. The findings align with the overall conclusion that phage resistance can affect multiple aspects of bacterial physiology.

result: The main conclusions of the study: infection by certain staphylococcal phages sensitizes MRSA strains to β-lactams with 10- to 1000-fold MIC reductions, phage-treated MRSA exhibit attenuated virulence (reduced hemolysis and clumping), and different MRSA strains evolved unique genetic profiles despite similar phenotypes.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'the findings are convincing' and the work 'improves our knowledge.' Reviewer 2 noted 'Phage-mediated re-sensitization to antibiotics has been reported previously but the underlying mutational analyses have not been described,' highlighting the novelty. Reviewer 3 stated 'the experiments that have been carried out are convincing' and 'In the current version of the manuscript, I find the study complete.' All reviewers accepted the main conclusions.
